One of the most sought-after products in Black Friday sales are Apple's iPads. These powerful tablets often cost a lot, and rarely see discounts, so a reduction in price becomes all the more tempting. But if you're just looking at the recent models, you're missing a trick.

Walmart is a major seller of restored iPads, or second-hand slates that have been professionally returned to a near-new condition. Tablets like this are often much cheaper than new ones, and work just as well (you can take my word for it, I bought a refurbished 2020 iPad Pro and it still works perfectly). While these models are cheaper anyway, Walmart is offering Black Friday deals on a fair few of them, bringing tablets down to remarkably cheap prices. These are mostly for older models, with a 2021 release the newest here, but they're still powerful and modern slates and so you might find an older iPad suits you fine.

Perhaps the best refurbished iPad deal is this: over a third off the price of a large-screen iPad. It's the 2020 model, but I can promise it still works fantastically since that's the one I own (and bought refurbed). I wish I could've found it at this price.

If you want a smaller iPad, this is the best deal for you; it's the only serious discount on an iPad mini, and 40% off is great. It's only the 64GB model, but one with cellular connection, so you can easily use cloud storage instead.

This is a much older iPad Pro, so you're buying this discount for the large screen rather than modern specs. It has more storage than many other of these refurbished models, at 128GB.

Another modern-build tablet in Walmart's refurb sales is this 2020 iPad Air, and its discount brings it to the lowest price of any home button-less model on this list. It's for the smaller 64GB model.

This is an older iPad, but it still works well (even without being restored), and so $140 is a really good price for it. The extra bargain is in the accessories you're getting with it: a protective case and charging cable are both included with the tablet.

If you've been looking for a new slate, changing tack in the Black Friday iPad deals to buy an older, refurbished model might seem might seem unthinkable.

Older slates work just well for tasks like word processing, streaming video, communications and simple workflow tasks. Slack has never challenged my 6-year-old iPad Pro. The trappings of newer slates, like advanced chipsets, will only really pay off for intensive tasks like video editing.

What about gaming? From my experience, older tablets still run the most advanced games pretty well. After all, game makers don't want to limit their potential audience by excluding owners of older tech, so they optimize their games to work well on various devices.

The only problem with older tablets is that they are less battery-efficient, even in refurbished models which usually enjoy new batteries. Basically any game more complex than NYT Games will sap battery quite quickly, so I only game on my iPad when I'm at home and near a power supply.

So if you're weighing up between an old or new slate, where you plan to play is the big thing worth considering.

If you're considering rivals, we've also got a round-up of the best gaming tablets, so you can see how iPads stack up against Android counterparts.

#3923. Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

#3922. Phil Spencer Might Not Be At Xbox Anymore, But He's Still Playing Loads Of Games

Phil Spencer is a legend of the Xbox division, having helped redefine the brand after a disastarous Xbox One launch in 2013, and spearheading such initiatives as Xbox Game Pass, Xbox backwards compatibility, crossplay, and a renewed focus on gaming rather than continuing the push towards "TV, TV, TV" that had proven so controversial.

It's very possible that without his influence, Xbox would have shut its doors over a decade ago.

News Microsoft Considered Pulling The Plug On Xbox Back In 2014

We haven't heard anything from Spencer since he announced his retirement earlier in 2026, but he's still very actively playing games on his Xbox consoles, including some of this year's new releases.

For example, he's racked up 940/1000 gamerscore in Echo Generation 2, 650/1000 in Forza Horizon 6, 585/1000 in Replaced, and he's also been playing the likes of Halo: Campaign Evolved, Gears of War: E-Day, Sopa - Tale of the Stolen Potato, Baldur's Gate 3, Vampire Crawlers and even Sunset Overdrive in recent months.

One of Phil's most beloved qualities as Xbox boss was that he proved himself to be a hardcore gamer, being someone who actively seeks to play games in his spare time. New Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is somewhat the opposite, admitting back in February that she doesn't "pretend to be the best gamer" and that it's ultimately not her goal to be.

Anyway, Phil is busy enjoying his retirement right now, and we wish him all the best from everyone here at Pure Xbox. We unfortunately never got a chance to meet the man ourselves, but always admired his leadership from afar.

Here's hoping he might start hitting the interview circuit and doing what the likes of Peter Moore and Nintendo's Reggie Fils-Aimé have done in the past, as we'd love to see him sticking around the industry in some capacity going forward.

1.9.0 races in with new Knockout Tour routes, too

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mario Kart World just got a massive new update in version 1.9.0, finally bringing Nintendo's Switch 2 racing game into the limelight – but not all fans are satisfied.

Nintendo unveils 1.9.0 in a colorful trailer on YouTube, featuring eight "new" tracks and two Knockout Tour routes – and yes, the quote marks around the word "new" are intentional on my part. That's because the tracks are sequels of sorts, acting as the "two" counterparts to already existing maps: Airship Fortress 2, Desert Hills 2, DK Pass 2, Maio Bros. Circuit 2, Koopa Troopa Beach 2, Salty Salty Speedway 2, and Wario Stadium 2.

Fans are jokingly calling 1.9.0 the "update of 2s" in the comments, noting that there isn't one truly new map in the lineup here. They're just reverse takes on old tracks, really. "This update certainly has 'The Power of Two' in it," reads one reply. Another jests, "This is like if McDonald's slapped a McChicken inside a McDouble, put it in a new box, and called it a brand-new menu item," clarifying they're "not mad at this update, though."

There is still 2.0 to look forward to, after all – and players note that's likely why Nintendo hasn't dropped anything too big in 1.9.0. "People don't seem to realize we're getting close to a 2.0 update," as one response puts it. "That's the big one that will have a lot of stuff that probably people are looking for and stuff that people aren't expecting." As for the Knockout Tour routes, this week's patch also brings two: Feather Rally and Lucky Cat Rally.

The new version includes plenty of other changes, as outlined on Nintendo's official support website. They range from technical to wholesome, like the fact that "confetti now falls during the results presentation in Grand Prix and Knockout Tour." Folks can also now pass through the river route to Cheep Cheep Falls from DK Pass, Sky-High Sundae, Salty Salty Speedway, Starview Peak, and Wario Shipyard.

All in all, it's not a bad update – heck, at least it's something seeing the love Nintendo's given Mario Kart 8 recently – but it does leave ample room for a banger 2.0, if you ask me.

#3920. Star Trek: Voyager - Across The Unknown Final DLC Ventures To Switch 2 Next Month

The Year of Hell is right around the corner

Daedalic Entertainment and GameXcite are wrapping up the bonus content for Star Trek: Voyager - Across The Unknown with one final wave of DLC.

The 'Year of Hell' expansion launches on Switch 2 next month on 9th December, with its own mini-campaign inspired by the Voyager two-parter of the same name.

In it, you'll be up against Captain Annorax and his civilisation-destroying time ship. You can either follow the critical path from the show and help Janeway & co. take down this baddie, or you can try something new and attempt to strike a deal with him.

This is its own storyline focused on survival gameplay, so your main game save will remain untouched for its duration.

Here's a brief rundown of the expansion's key features and a handful of screenshots:

Manage the decline. Gameplay turned on its head. Begin with advanced systems and upgrades already in place, then fight to keep essential systems operational as the Krenim take that advantage away. A year of losses and difficult sacrifices. Attacks can destroy rooms, tear entire decks from the ship, and kill crew members. With less space and fewer resources, success means seeing how many of your crew survive the twelve months. Six ships. Shifting loyalties. Face four Krenim vessels, including Annorax’s timeship. The Mawasi Cruiser and Nihydron Warship can join your forces in certain timeline branches-or turn their weapons on you in others.

Those who already own the Across the Unknown expansion pass will land the DLC automatically at launch.

We had a great time with the base game earlier this year, calling it a damn good time "for resource management and survival nuts who like a bit of '90s Trek" in our 8/10 review.

If the wait for EA’s upcoming Marvel’s Iron Man is proving too tough to take, then Wuthering Waves’ forthcoming milestone v4.0 update may scratch your Tony Stark itch.

In this exclusive IGN footage of the gacha game’s new ‘Embers of Everbright’ arc – scheduled to release on 22nd December – dev Kuro has introduced the new Strider Mechsuit.

The new utility factors in both combat and exploration, and the studio says:

“Beyond combat, Version 4.0 introduces exciting new opportunities for open-world exploration, allowing players to pilot the Strider Mechsuit with full 360-degree mobility, take to the skies and traverse the region with greater freedom.”

But the new update will not only explore the skies – you’ll also be able to go underwater as well, massively increasing the scope of the sandbox.

Kuro says its new ‘Chapter of the Year’ format will span multiple updates, so expect a bigger, deeper narrative set to unfold over the course of 2027 here.

Two new characters that will feature in that story are Anna and Lucielle, and you can get a glimpse of their respective combat in the trailer above.

Again, it all looks amazing, with the time being the only thing holding me back from these many, many games at this point.

Kuro says it’ll reveal more about v4.0 ahead of its release next month, but this is just a first taste to whet your appetite.

#3918. Unity launches new Fellowship program, offering a "no recoup" $50,000 grant to indie developers planning to launch their game in the next 12 months

Unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that plan release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the company has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental issues.

Unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

The grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

#3917. Capcom Is Delisting Exoprimal In A Few Months, Then Killing It In 2027

Can't believe the dinosaurs are going extinct, again!

Capcom has today announced that its dinosaur PvPvE shooter Exoprimal will end service on September 29, 2027, meaning it will no longer be playable after that date. The game is also set to be delisted from digital storefronts, including the Xbox Store, on March 30, 2027.

"We regret to announce that service for Exoprimal will be discontinued as of 8:00 PM (PDT) on Wednesday, September 29, 2027."

Exoprimal launched on Xbox Series X|S on July 14, 2023, and suffered a pretty pants opening with only 4,995 players logging in through Steam to play Capcom's new team-based shooter.

Here's a detailed breakdown of what is going to happen to Exoprimal in the months leading to end of service:

Following Capcom's mighty 2026 releases, Resident Evil Requiem and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, I wanted to understand what went wrong for Exoprimal, so I hopped back on. Funnily enough, I was actually enjoying the game, despite it being a ghost town. Only nine players were active at the time, and it really felt like it. It's still a fun title though, which makes the end of service announcement quite sad, at least for me.

#3916. Simon Pegg turned up early to The Rings of Power set so he could voice the Balrog's scenes opposite Charlie Vickers' Sauron

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Bringing all the latest movie news, features, and reviews to your inbox

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Exclusive: The Rings of Power season 3 episode 7 director breaks down the Balrog sequence

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Simon Pegg voices the Balrog in The Rings of Power season 3 episode 7, bringing the iconic creature to life. His climactic scene comes opposite Sauron, who comes to ask him the secrets of forging the One Ring in the fires of Mount Doom and surviving.

Pegg actually came on set to film the sequence with Charlie Vickers, according to the episode's director Stefan Schwartz, which added another layer to the sequence. Despite being told they wouldn't get to his bit until after lunch, Schwartz says Pegg turned up in the morning, and during every break in filming they'd speak through the history of the Balrog.

Then during the sequence with Sauron, Pegg was present on set with a microphone, speaking the Balrog's lines. "Charlie had to look at this big light on the crane that was moving around where the Balrog was going to go," Schwartz explains. "So Charlie was looking there, but Simon was actually working with him, and we could rehearse it and play it in different ways."

He adds: "It was really nice to have him there on set, and all of it was played opposite him. And in fact, towards the end, for their tête-à-tête, Simon was right there, and it really felt they were definitely acting with each other rather than in a vacuum, which could so easily happen."

Bringing the Balrog visually to the screen was another challenge for the director too. "The tricky thing with the Balrog was we don't ever see the Balrog very much in anything before, and it needs to express emotion and anger and coolness," he explains.

"We worked out that the Balrog would have these different colors. It would be a cooler color, then it would warm up as it got angry or as it was getting emotional, and then start really flaming when it was angry."

The final result is impressive, and the flaming monster is a real highlight of episode 7. For more of a deep dive into the iconic crafting of the One Ring, check out what the director had to say about the "pressure" of bringing it to the screen.

#3915. You've Basically Got to Wait an Entire Year to Play Showa American Story

Here is an incredibly far-off release date you can pencil in (and then probably rub out because it'll be delayed again): the wild and wacky Showa American Story is coming to PS5 on 28th October 2027.

It was originally planned to launch in 2026, so this is a pretty substantial delay to the game, but the "core game content" is now complete, according to the developer.

The next 11 months will be dedicated to "polishing and optimizing the experience so that when you step into Showa American Story, it feels cohesive, responsive, and complete".

Preview Forget the Soulslikes, This Bizarre New PS5 Game Is Channelling Shenmue Instead

For those who don't know, Showa American Story is based on the scenario where "Japan has bought out most of the United States with its strong economic power. A surge of immigration has firmly planted Japanese culture within the American continent. Two cultures are rapidly amalgamated, although conflicts are inevitable, citizens gradually adapt to a life never imagined as time goes by."

This leads to a bizarre adventure, which we got a small taste of at Gamescom earlier this year. You play Chigusa Choko, a female movie star brought back from the dead who sets out on a quest with vibes of Shenmue, Yakuza, and No More Heroes.

What we played was incredibly unfinished and janky, but there was still some promise on show. Let's hope almost a year of polish and further work on the game turns it into a strong experience.

Can you wait that long to play Showa American Story? Let us know in the comments below.

#3914. Final Fantasy Resonance Devs Are Somehow Surprised That Fans Still Like Turn-Based Combat

"I expected opinions on it might be divided"

Final Fantasy Resonance was met with high praise when it launched on 22nd October 2026, earning a score of 8/10 from us and a critic average of 85 over on Metacritic.

Despite being an adaptation of a somewhat middling mobile title, Resonance's focus on turn-based combat mixed with the handsome HD-2D visuals made it an instant fan-favourite. The developers, however, seem somehow surprised at the positive reception, believing that opinions would be a bit more divided.

This comes via an interview at Game Spark with producer Keisuke Nakashima, co-producer Miki Kimura, and director Hiroto Furuya (thanks, Automaton), who all feel that Resonance's reception exceeded their expectations.

Nakanishi-san said, “I think the action-oriented and 3D Final Fantasy games are wonderful too, but I was surprised to see just how many people, not only in Japan but overseas as well, are eager for the kind of FF they remember from back in the day, with classic turn-based battles and pixel art.”

Development actually focused on appealing to more old-school fans of the series, with Nakanishi stating that the intended direction was for Resonance to feel almost like a follow-up to Final Fantasy 6. "We figured it was something we ourselves would enjoy, and that there would be players out there who’d feel the same way", he said.

With the series being so heavily focused on 3D visuals and action-oriented gameplay in recent years, the team simply didn't expect Resonance to have such mainstream appeal.

"I thought this was a rather unconventional title, so I expected opinions on it might be divided", said Kimura-san. "I think the fact that a game with such an unusual background has been embraced by so many people is a positive for the industry as a whole, and I’m personally very happy to see it.”

Hopefully the positive reception will lead to more original games being made that focus on turn-based combat and 'retro' visuals. There's clearly a demand for it!

#3913. "Games are best made by people": The IWGB and other European unions publish joint manifesto calling on workers, employers and consumers to reject genAI

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people."

The manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture."

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games."

It's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable."

#3912. The Witcher 4 Dev Signs New 'Agreements' With Sony, But What Does It Mean For Xbox?

"This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook"

Michał Nowakowski has also now shared the following tweet about this:

Original Story: Last night, we saw some news starting to do the rounds about The Witcher 4 and its developer CD Projekt Red, with Chief Financial Officer Piotr Nielubowicz stating that the studio has entered into new "agreements" with Sony.

These agreements cover the presence of CDPR games on subscription services such as PlayStation Plus, but also "our collaboration during the upcoming Witcher 4 marketing campaign" - which is the bit we're particularly interested in.

Here's a bit of the transcription via our friends at VGC:

"Just today, we signed new partnership agreements with Sony Interactive Entertainment covering the presence of our games on PlayStation and in PlayStation Plus subscriptions, as well as our collaboration during the upcoming Witcher 4 marketing campaign."

"This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook in this and future years."

A lot of people are now speculating that The Witcher 4's "collaboration" with Sony may be akin to what Take-Two has done with GTA 6, pushing the whole "plays best on PS5" campaign and restricting how Xbox is allowed to advertise the game. For example, GTA's launch trailer was solely focused around PS5 for an exclusive window.

It's important to highlight that this is just speculation though, and there may be aspects of these agreements that aren't exclusive at all. We've seen CDPR titles like Cyberpunk 2077 on Xbox Game Pass in the not too distant past, for example, so the PlayStation Plus agreement doesn't necessarily mean Game Pass is out the window.

Let's wait and see what happens with this, but just keep in mind that we could be looking at a situation where The Witcher 4 gets a bigger push on PlayStation than Xbox when it (hopefully) releases in 2028. We'll also leave you with a fun GTA comparison quote from joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski about the difference between Witcher 3 and 4!

"I’m not going to make a deep dive, full-blown review of GTA 5 versus GTA 6, but of course, we did look at the game, we did see the differences... we believe there’s going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4. It’s been 11 years. We are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better-looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game."

It's happening. We have some more movement on Lords of the Fallen 2 from CI Games. No, there still isn't a release date, but we know when we're getting one. The action RPG sequel is now due to arrive slightly later than previously announced, but still in the first half of 2027, and we'll be hearing more quite soon.

Marek Tyminski, the CEO of CI Games, reveals the details himself. "Lords of the Fallen 2: April 2027," he writes on Twitter. "Exact date in December."

What Tyminski's post doesn't specify this that this is actually another delay. The game was originally due in the back half of this year, before moving to the first quarter of 2027. While it's slightly annoying to only get an announcement for the announcement, at least we know we don't have long to wait to find out when exactly Lords of the Fallen 2 is coming out. Knowing the release month is very helpful too.

Lords of the Fallen II: April 2027. Exact date in December. https://t.co/yYaevDqaxeNovember 24, 2026

I could be wrong here, of course, but that seems to all but guarantee the game's presence at The Game Awards. Trailers and reveals are always a big part of the show, and I'm not sure where else we might see the follow-up otherwise, unless CI Games is planning some sort of livestream of its own we're not yet aware of.

Regardless of the delay, this is all pretty quick turnaround for the release, since Lords of the Fallen 2 was only announced during the Opening Night Live of Gamescom 2025. Maybe I'm just jaded from increasingly elongated announcement schedules for blockbuster games, but getting the release window only a year and a half after the formal reveal is pretty tight by today's standards.

I mean, we just waited years to find out what the full title of The Elder Scrolls 6 is. We'll see what CI Games has to offer come December, which, at time of writing, is just six days away. Maybe Mariah Carey will be involved in some way. I doubt it, but imagine. I bet she loves a bit of Lords of the Fallen, honestly.

#3910. I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that big a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in New York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

Sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

You could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

They often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

The latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

They aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

#3909. GTA 6 Performs Better on Xbox Series X Than Base PS5, Despite All of Sony's Marketing

Even though Sony has paid god-only-knows how much money to market GTA 6 as a borderline PS5 exclusive, it turns out that Rockstar's magnum opus actually runs better on Xbox.

This is according to those tech wizards over at Digital Foundry, who have spent hours comparing the open world title across base PS5, PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S.

Now, we already know that GTA 6 isn't perfect on the standard PS5. It suffers from minor but sometimes prolonged frame rate drops during busy scenes — whether you're speeding through heavy traffic or fighting for your life in a particularly explosive combat encounter.

But in a rather shocking twist, the Xbox Series X outdoes the PS5 in this department. While Digital Foundry's testing shows that the frame rate dips are still present on the Series X, they're nowhere near as frequent.

They write: "PS5 suffers substantially more frequent frame rate drops than Series X, which is compounded by the fact that the Xbox machine also benefits from 120Hz VRR support to smooth out minor dips."

The article continues: "Ultimately, Series X is meaningfully better off."

This isn't what you'd expect, given that every PlayStation-related GTA 6 advertisement and trailer has boasted that the game 'Plays Best on PS5'.

Okay, so that slogan might technically be true if we're counting the PS5 Pro, where GTA 6 does perform best by some distance, thanks to a combination of the console's PSSR upscaler and increased GPU power.

But on base hardware, it's Microsoft that wins out.

"Overall, the PS5 Pro leads the rankings with its superior visual detail and rock-solid 30fps target, followed by the Xbox Series X — which edges out the standard PS5 through better performance stability," Digital Foundry concludes.

Are you surprised by these findings? Have you noticed any frequent frame rate drops in GTA 6 on PS5? Wonder if we'll ever see 60fps again in the comments section below.

@Rich33 Yes fully agree. It's almost certain that adding FSR 4 on Xbox (and QSSR on PS5) would make the game run at worse frame rates. To compensate for that they could lower the BASE resolution (currently 1440p on both consoles) and hope the upscaler does a better job than their current solution.

But both of these techniques are pretty computationally expensive, taking up around 10-15% of total frame budget at 30fps -> 4K. To get FSR 4 working on Series S, which has a similar CPU to Series X, they had to lower the base resolution to 720p. That may not be worth it.

#3908. Former Dishonored designer joins the team on New Blood's Victorian immersive sim Gloomwood, with a new level and new weapons coming this year

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by New Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The update is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

#3907. One Of The Most Successful VR Games Of All Time Is Coming To Xbox In January 2027

Say hello to the flatscreen version of Arizona Sunshine

If you've ever owned any kind of VR headset in your life, you've probably come across a game known as Arizona Sunshine, and we're pleased to say that its new flatscreen version is coming to Xbox Series X and Series S in January!

This is a zombie apocalypse game that served as one of the most successful examples of a proper single-player FPS in the early VR era, first releasing all the way back in 2016. It's obviously received a lot of changes for the Xbox release, most notably in the form of a new third-person perspective rather than sticking with first-person.

Its story focuses around a survivor called "Sunny" and his dog known as "Buddy", the latter of which is now playable in two-player co-op as of this new release. Don't be fooled by Buddy's cuteness though - it's still a gory game and certainly not intended for kids, so just keep that in mind before you hit the purchase button or the trailer up above!

Anyway, Arizona Sunshine was a big deal 10 years ago, so it'll be fascinating to see how well it fares on modern non-VR platforms. The game is already available to pre-order on the Xbox Store at a low price of £21.99 / $24.99, and it also seemingly comes with Xbox Play Anywhere support (meaning you get a free PC copy too).

We'll leave you with more details on Arizona Sunshine below, launching for Xbox on January 21st of 2027.

Sharpen your machete and grab your friends. Arizona Sunshine® brings its award-winning zombie apocalypse to explosive third-person action, featuring online and split-screen co-op, brutal combat, dark humor, and Buddy, your loyal zombie-chomping canine companion.

#3906. Kevin Feige confirms what Marvel diehards suspected: Avengers: Secret Wars is set on Battleworld

The Marvel boss goes weapon free on Secret Wars' premise

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige has all but confirmed the setting for Avengers: Secret Wars and its "imagination gone wild" premise.

Speaking to Entertainment Weekly, Feige described Secret Wars – arriving one year after Avengers: Doomsday as a "launching pad for our films in 2028" as they begin "a very new era at that point."

2028 will see Marvel release X-Men, Ghost Rider, and Black Panther 3, but in the here-and-now, Feige (usually a brick wall when it comes to spoilers) is happy to reveal that Secret Wars will be set on Battleworld.

Not familiar with the location? Taking its name from the 1984 and 2015 comics of the same name, Battleworld was first depicted as a planet overseen by the Beyonder for his goal of making several heroes and villains fight.

The 2015 iteration is closer to what we'll likely see in the MCU – a jumbled patchwork planet brought together by Doctor Doom after the collapse of the multiverse. Fragments of different times, realities and locations are all able to co-exist in one space, and is ruled by Doom.

"Secret Wars is different than any other movie we’ve ever made," Feige teased. "Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie Secret Wars takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what’s exciting about it."

"It’s such a major storyline, it needed two movies to tell that story," co-director Joe Russo added. "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Feige even went one further, saying the comics Secret Wars is based on (the two Secret Wars events and Jonathan Hickman's 'Time Runs Out') could be used to work out spoilers for the next two MCU crossovers.

"If you wanted spoilers for The Odyssey, you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for Doomsday and Secret Wars, you can go look at the comics. It is very much the same thing that we’re doing, which is the fun of what happens in the culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event, and what Doctor Doom does next," Feige said. "And that very much is what Secret Wars is."

Prior to Secret Wars stepping into Battleworld, Avengers: Doomsday hits UK cinemas on December 16 and US cinemas on December 18.

#3905. Embracer begin yet another round of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, while they're still midway through development on two Tomb Raider games

Update: Studio confirms eight staff lost their jobs

Update 18/11: Crystal Dynamics have provided the following statement to RPS, confirming it cut eight staff members:

As initially reported by Vertical Slice (thanks, Chris!), the workforce of Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics is being cut as part of a new set of layoffs by owners Embracer. As far as is currently known, those affected include senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, and UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, all of whom shared news of their redunancies on LinkedIn. There may be more affected, but neither Crystal Dynamics nor Embracer have offered comments on the reduction of staff as yet.

This now marks the studio's fifth round of layoffs since Embracer acquired it in 2022, following cuts in March 2025, August 2025, November 2025, and March this year. This is a drastic amount even considering the current state of the industry, with layoffs seemingly happening several times a week, but unfortunately, this is par for the course for Embracer. Even still, it makes one wonder just how many staff are left at Crystal Dynamics by now. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis and Tomb Raider: Catalyst are still in production, so you'd hope that the studio won't be shuttered entirely.

According to Legacy of Atlantis' Steam page, generative AI has been used in the development of Legacy of Atlantis "to support some early exploration and temporary development content. Any AI-assisted assets were either replaced or refined by humans in order to maintain the creative and artistic vision of the development team." I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

#3904. Sony Will Support The Witcher 4's Marketing, Much Like GTA 6

The Witcher 4 dev CDPR has signed a marketing arrangement with Sony, which will likely see the latter promote the upcoming RPG similarly to GTA 6.

PlayStation pushed Rockstar’s latest release ridiculously hard, claiming it ‘Plays Best on PS5’.

While that may only actually apply to the PS5 Pro version, the Japanese giant could argue that its base hardware – which drops a few more frames than the Xbox Series X – still has the advantage of deeper DualSense integration et al.

Irrespective of slogan, CDPR’s CFO Piotr Nielubowicz told investors today that his company recently signed a new arrangement with Sony, which includes “the presence of our games on PlayStation and in PS Plus subscriptions, as well as our collaboration during the upcoming The Witcher 4 marketing campaign”.

Nielubowicz didn’t clarify whether this will be an exclusive marketing arrangement, but fans with good memories may recall the first footage of The Witcher 4 was presented on PS5.

With Microsoft owning a chunk of the Western RPG development scene, this seems like a shrewd move by Sony to me.

It’ll want to present CDPR’s next title as a major PlayStation title, because there’s still a possibility the next Elder Scrolls may skip its system entirely. (Although Xbox isn’t currently saying either way.)

Obviously we’ll need to wait and see how deep this partnership runs, but if it’s anything like Sony’s GTA 6 campaign, then it’ll be very aggressive to say the least.

#3903. Sony defeat $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit which argued PlayStation's dominant market position fuels "excessive and unfair" game prices

It's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the company of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

It's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

In a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

As if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another big game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

#3902. Sci-fi RPG Exodus continues evoking Mass Effect by revealing female lead and nicknaming her FemJun

Sci-fi role-playing game Exodus continues to play into the Mass Effect comparisons by revealing the female version of its main character Jun, and with studio Archetype referring to her in marketing material as FemJun.

If that moniker sounds familiar it's because it is: the female Commander Shepard character in the Mass Effect series was nicknamed FemShep. FemShep became an iconic part of BioWare's iconic series, eventually proving that female leads could front games just as successfully as male leads could, and be every bit as popular.

Is the nickname FemJun too blatant? Possibly. But there's well publicised BioWare pedigree at Archetype Entertainment, in the studio's co-founders and in the people leading the project. Key Mass Effect writer Drew Karpyshyn is in charge of writing Exodus, for example, and the similarities to Mass Effect are something the Exodus team has not been shy about in the past. In the wake of Mass Effect 5 being cancelled and BioWare being closed, they become even more alluring.

There are, however, big and important differences between Exodus and Mass Effect, key among them, time dilation. In Exodus, there are special Exodus missions whereby you leave your home planet and fly far away, and in doing so experience time differently to the people back home. Many years will pass for them while only days will pass for you, which provides the game with a way to show you long-term consequences of your actions when you return.

Archetype hasn't shown the female version of Jun before, despite having released many videos of Exodus, perhaps to build anticipation for her reveal. It's a press beat that's also provided Archetype - a studio owned by Dungeons & Dragons company Wizards of the Coast - with an occasion to reveal the two actors playing Jun in the game.

Female Jun is portrayed by Carina Conti, who played the lead in the recent Mafia game, The Old Country - Isabella Torrisi. She's appeared in HBO's Winning Time and Hulu/Freeform's Good Trouble as well. Male Jun, meanwhile, is portrayed by Stephen Oyoung, who played Mister Negative in Insomniac's Marvel's Spider-Man 1 and 2 games, and Red Hood in Gotham Knights. He also appeared in Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, The Wrecking Crew, and Twisters. The game also famously stars Matthew McConaughey.

Archetype announced a Dark Horse hardback art book to go on sale alongside the game next year as well. This arrives a week after the game; Exodus arrives 7th April 2027 on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X, and the art book on 13th April.

Matt played Exodus at Gamescom relatively recently and came away impressed, referring to it as "the best kind of surprise". "I wasn't expecting quite such a bombastic 45 minutes when I first picked up a controller and settled into Exodus, admittedly, but the more I played, the more it made sense," he wrote. "I might not be much of a Mass Effect fan (damn you M35 Mako once more), but Exodus is now firmly on my radar ahead of its arrival next year."

#3900. Super Boss Monster review

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I was a fan of the original Boss Monster, so I enjoyed Super Boss Monster as well. It’s a superior version of a fun, relatively quick game. There’s enough strategy to keep advanced board game fans interested, but simple enough for newcomers and younger fans to enjoy as well.

Fixes many of its predecessors' shortcomings

Compatible with Boss Monster and expansions

New town board ensures players will always have options every round

Players tend to gang up on whoever's winning

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

Boss Monster, first released in 2013, is a quick-paced card game that puts players on the monster’s side of a dungeon crawl. As the name would suggest, it involves luring heroes into a dungeon and then killing them before they can reach the Boss Monster. Developer Brotherwise Games turned this into a steady franchise, releasing numerous expansions that added new spells and rooms to the equation.

However, now that's all been shaken up with the latest instalment – upgrading both the 8-bit pixel look to Super Nintendo-inspired 16-bit graphics as well as its gameplay. Super Boss Monster smooths over some of the rough edges of Boss Monster while remaining fully compatible with the previous version of the game. The result is a quick-paced experience that feels a bit more even than before but maintains most of its predecessor’s tenets. Is it one of the best card games, though?

Super Boss Monster features three separate decks of cards and a town board where heroes go shortly before adventuring to their doom. The first of these decks consists of Room cards, which players use to build their dungeon. Rooms are divided between trap rooms and monster rooms, along with their advanced counterparts. Each room has a damage figure and treasure on the bottom of the card. The damage determines how much damage a room deals to heroes, while the treasure helps to determine which heroes (if any) enter a player’s dungeon.

The second deck of cards is the spell deck, which comprise of instant use spells that are generally disruptive to the game. Most of these spells are cast during the adventure phase of the game and typically impose a negative effect, either by buffing a hero or by somehow negating effects in a player’s dungeon. Many spells are cast on other players, although there are some spells that have beneficial effects as well.

Players: 1-4Ages: 13+Game type: Drafting/hand-managementComplexity: LowLasts: 30minsDesigner: Hayden Dillard & Johnny O'NealPublisher: Brotherwise GamesPlay if you enjoy: Boss Monster, old-school video games

The final deck of cards is the hero deck, which comprises two tiers of heroes. Early on in the game, players will face standard heroes that have low health and limited abilities. As the game enters its final stage, players have to contend with epic heroes, which have even more health and can negate entire rooms in a dungeon. While epic heroes are harder to vanquish, they score more points than their standard counterparts.

All three decks were featured in the original Boss Monster, but the one new addition to Super Boss Monster is the town board. Heroes now populate on the town board, destined to either travel to a dungeon or linger in one of several special buildings. Each of these buildings also have minion slots, granting players a one-off action during the town phase. Drafting also takes place on the town board, with leftover cards remaining on the board until the next phase.

Super Boss Monster plays out over numerous rounds, with an unrelenting stream of heroes entering each player’s dungeon periodically. Each player starts with a hand of cards and a small one-room dungeon. Over the course of the game, players build out that dungeon to a total of five rooms and buff it either temporarily or permanently with various effects. Once a dungeon hits its allotted five rooms, a player’s Boss Monster levels up, granting them new abilities.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

Boss Monster plays very similarly to Super Boss Monster, save for the opening Town Phase round. During this initial round, Heroes enter town and the Market is restocked with new rooms and spells. Starting with the first player (a signifier that rotates each round), players then place their Minion on either a town slot (or occasionally on a slot within their own dungeon) and drafts a new card from the market. One confusing part of the game is that the Minion effects don’t resolve immediately – players have to wait until a separate phase to gain their benefit.

After the town phase comes the Build phase, where players add to their dungeon. Builds happen simultaneously and are technically secret, as the results often determine which heroes enter which dungeon. Players choose a card from their hand and play it face down onto their dungeon. Once all players have chosen their rooms, they simultaneously reveal them.

One thing I like about Super Boss Monster is that players don’t have to spend resources to add a room to their dungeon. Basic Trap and Monster Rooms can be played during any round. Stronger Advanced rooms can only be played on top of existing rooms that share a treasure icon with the existing room. Advanced rooms often have more treasure than basic rooms, along with more powerful abilities. However, placing an Advanced room essentially resets that room, removing any buffs from that space.

If strategic card games are your thing, it's worth checking out Wingspan Pocket. It has all the brilliance of the original, but with far fewer barriers to entry. As for a more fantastical strategy game, it's worth checking out Gwent: The Legendary Card Game.

After the Build phase comes the Minion phase, when players gain their benefit of whatever space they placed their minion. Minion effects range from gaining a temporary piece of treasure to the dungeon (which can break ties and entice heroes to a certain dungeon) to drawing extra cards. One of my favorite minion effects is the +2 effect. When a hero moves to a specialty landmark, players can buff a hero with two additional health and send them to any dungeon. Although players can send a buffed hero to an opponent’s dungeon to hurt them, it’s also a way for players to gain extra points, especially when a glut of heroes show up that don’t want to enter your dungeon. This is one of the big improvements from Boss Monster, as there are now ways to get a steady stream of heroes into the dungeon even when the treasure doesn’t fall their way.

Once the Minion phase is complete, the heroes finally enter the dungeon. Players determine which heroes enter which dungeon by determining which dungeon has the most of a hero’s preferred treasure type. Players can pursue one of two strategies to attract heroes; they can either dominate one or two treasure types or go for a more balanced approach that relies on careful deployment of minion powers. Both strategies come with their own advantages, although it may be easier to dominate one type of treasure in higher player count games.

Once heroes deploy to the dungeon, players take turns seeing whether their dungeons are strong enough to vanquish them. Heroes progress from room to room, with rooms dealing damage first and then resolving room effects. One thing to keep track of is that many effects add temporary damage to rooms. While damage counters are permanent effects and are represented by markers, they’re separate from temporary buffs that typically last for one round of play. Pay careful attention to which cards specify placing damage counters and which add temporary buffs to the game, as this can be a touch confusing to track.

If a hero is vanquished, players flip their card over and place them under their boss monster – they’ve been defeated and converted into a soul gem. However, if a hero clears the dungeon, they remain face up and are slotted under the boss monster, representing damage taken by the boss monster during the game. The game ends once a player collects ten soul gems (regardless of how much damage they’ve taken) or when the hero deck runs out. Each soul gem counts as a positive point, while each point of damage is a negative point. The winner is the player with the most victory points at the end.

Super Boss Monster is essentially a polished version of Boss Monster that addresses some of the biggest shortcomings of its predecessor. Players have more ways to lure heroes into dungeons beyond dominating a specific type of treasure, which removes some of the frustrations of a poor series of drafts. However, the game still has the Munchkin-like feature of being able to gang up on a frontrunner, which leads to an element of kingmaking when a player is essentially eliminated from winning.

Probably my biggest frustration of Super Boss Monster is that, when played on its own, the cards are rather limited. This is because the game’s fully compatible with its predecessors, so you can simply grab older expansions in order to get a more varied experience. An expansion for Super Boss Monster is also due out this year, so there’s plenty of ways to get more out of this game once the base version starts to feel repetitive.

✅ You enjoy a fast-paced tableau builder game: Super Boss Monster isn’t too complicated and takes only about 30 minutes to play through.✅ You get nostalgic for 16-bit video games: Super Boss Monster celebrates old-school video games, with plenty of references to other video game franchises. ✅ You enjoyed the original Boss Monster: Super Boss Monster largely keeps to the original Boss Monster formula, with some improvements.

❌ You don’t like Munchkin-style shenanigans: The lead player will get targeted with a lot of unfair effects and there’s little they can do to stop it. ❌ You don’t like simple strategy games: The strategy of Super Boss Monster is simplistic in nature, largely limited to figuring out when and where to place rooms. Deeper strategy fans might find this game too simplistic.

This review was conducted using a sample provided by the publisher. For more details on our process, check how we test board games or the GamesRadar+ reviews policy.

Christian is an experienced freelance journalist who has been covering the tabletop gaming industry for years. He specializes in coverage of Dungeons & Dragons, the Pokemon Trading Card Game, and Warhammer.

#3899. PS5 RPG Lords of the Fallen 2 Locks on to April 2027 Release Date Following Lengthy Delay

Lords of the Fallen 2 is officially targeting an April 2027 release date, having been hit with a lengthy delay back in the summer.

The anticipated action RPG was previously eyeing an autumn / fall 2026 launch, which would have only added to an insane PS5 schedule. Shifting to a vague 'Q1 2027' window seemed a wise move at the time.

And as mentioned, it's now going to land right towards the end of said quarter, which should give the game some room to breathe given that we're currently looking at very busy January, February, and March.

Interestingly, we'll be getting a more specific April date in the coming weeks, as an announcement is planned for December.

I'm guessing it'll be at The Game Awards? We're due a fresh look at this one either way.

Expectations are fairly high for this sequel. Its predecessor showed clear potential, but needed a huge number of updates to really shine; the suggestion is that Lords of the Fallen 2 will build on everything the last game did well, and be rock solid right out of the gate.
